intro: Advice from SME members and the faculty we talk to, for students in manufacturing, quality and engineering technology. Have a tip? Post it in the Discord and an officer will add it here.

tips.title: Start with a Green Belt, not a Black Belt
points: Belts go White, Yellow, Green, Black, then Master Black Belt. A Green Belt matches what a new grad actually does: help on improvement projects and run the basic tools (DMAIC, SIPOC, control charts, Gage R&R).

A senior-project professor here who spent his career at Toyota says students should go for a Green Belt. A Black Belt means you have led real improvement projects, and a new grad usually has not, so experienced engineers and hiring managers may question it.
A Black Belt is not fake. It is real and recognized. It is just weak without project experience behind it.

tips.title: Who issues the belt matters more than the color
points: There is no single official Six Sigma body, so belts from different issuers are not equal. Quality engineers will look at who issued it.
ASQ (CSSGB) is the best-known Green Belt, but it requires 3 years of full-time work experience in the subject, so most students cannot take it yet. Plan on it after you start working.
IASSC Green Belt has no prerequisites: one proctored, closed-book exam (100 questions, 3 hours, 70% to pass, about $350). It is the strongest option you can take as a student.

Online-only providers such as MSI (Management and Strategy Institute) certify by online exam plus a project simulation, with no real project required for Black Belt. They are often discounted on deal sites. Faculty advice here: it is worth about what you paid for it.
A belt your employer trains you for, with a real project on their line, beats all of the above. Many manufacturers run their own programs.

tips.title: How to show it on a resume
points: Do not lead with it. Put it in a Certifications section near the bottom, not at the top or in your headline. A Lean Six Sigma professor here gives the same advice, even for students who earned a Black Belt.
Write the issuer and the year: "Lean Six Sigma Green Belt, IASSC, 2026".
What gets you hired is a project with a number: "cut setup time 30% on the Spartan Signs line". Use class projects, club projects and internships to show you can use the tools.

tips.title: Tech 31 and Tech 145 overlap: study them together
points: QA/QC (Tech 31) and Lean Manufacturing and Six Sigma (Tech 145) share a lot: DMAIC, SIPOC, voice of the customer, CTQs, defects vs nonconformities, Gage R&R. Learning a tool once for both classes saves time.
Know the difference in focus: Lean goes after waste (overproduction is the big one), Six Sigma goes after variation and defects.

tips.title: TI-84 stats tricks
points: For infinity in normalcdf, type 1E99 with the EE key (2nd then comma). Do not use the ^ key; it gives a wrong answer.
Use Sx, not σx, when you have a sample.
Turn on DiagnosticOn (catalog) so LinReg shows r and r².

tips.title: Go on the tours and do a project
points: Company tours (Tesla, Rigetti this year) are the easiest way to see a real line and meet engineers. Bring questions and ask for a contact.
Join a club project like Spartan Signs or Ain't No Waymo. It gives you resume bullets with real numbers before your senior project starts.

tips.title: Watch your units if you change majors
points: Past 180 units, financial aid can place an Excessive Unit hold. If that happens, file a SAP appeal with a graduation plan early, before the semester starts. Check with Financial Aid for the current rules.
